html:
Japan's first railway, opened in 1872 between Shimbashi in Tokyo and the port of Yokohama, a line of about 29 kilometres. It was one of the first great projects of the new Meiji government.

The government borrowed money in London and hired British engineers, led by Edmund Morel. Engines and rails were imported from Britain. Some officials opposed it, and the army held some of the land it needed, so for one stretch the track was laid on an embankment built into the sea.

The Meiji Emperor rode the train at the opening ceremony in October 1872. The trip took under an hour, against most of a day on foot. 14 October is still Railway Day in Japan.

The line became the start of the Tōkaidō line, which reached Kobe in 1889 along the old Tōkaidō road. Japan soon trained its own engineers and built its own engines. Its rail network grew into one of the densest in the world, and in 1964 it opened the Shinkansen, the first high-speed line.
